about.label: 01 — About
about.heading: About me
about.motto: Courage is not an absence of fear. Courage is fear walking.
about.p1: I'm Chia-Hung (Oscar) Lin, from Douliu, Yunlin. I began in the Department of Medical Sociology and Social Work, later transferred to Psychology, and completed two credit programs, in Child Development & Early Intervention and in Art Therapy, before graduating from Kaohsiung Medical University in June 2026.
about.p2: After graduating, I worked as contract staff at the Department of Social Affairs, Yunlin County Government, and served as staff at a youth representatives' workshop. Over those days, I watched the young people push past their limits in a short time; some of them have disabilities, and seeing them support and help one another felt deeply warm and left me hopeful about their futures. It made me surer of the path I want: to become a child clinical psychologist who walks alongside children as they grow. Next, I plan to apply to a graduate program in clinical psychology.
about.p3: I'm careful and organized: I set goals, sort out the order, and work through things one by one, double-checking before I hand anything in. With people, I try to be gentle, and when someone needs it, I'm glad to be the one who listens. When I make a mistake, I reflect on it and work out how to do better next time.
about.p4: I hope to be someone who is willing to try. You don't have to wait until you're unafraid to set out; you can walk forward, fear and all.
about.note: Outside of work, I love aviation; that's where this site's altimeter and flight route come from. In my free time, I also enjoy watching F1 and listening to music.

proj.label: 04 — Personal Project
proj.heading: Notedly
proj.sub: AI-Powered Read-Later App for iPhone & iPad | Personal Project, Built with Claude Code | Oct – Nov 2026
proj.intro: I came up with the idea, planned it, directed the work, tested it, and launched it; the code was written by the AI coding assistant Claude Code.
proj.b1: Zero to launch: Launched an iOS/iPadOS app on the App Store in 11 days (Oct 23–Nov 3), available in 174 countries and regions in 5 languages; released version 1.1 the day after launch.
proj.b2: Product planning: Defined and prioritized features, writing test steps for each one; shipped link and screenshot saving with text recognition, AI summaries and auto-categorization, a saved-places map, and cloud sync across iPhone and iPad. The codebase is about 9,400 lines.
proj.b3: Real-device testing: Tested every feature on my own iPhone and iPad, including field-testing location-based reminders outdoors, and requested fixes based on the results.
proj.b4: Launch and business setup: Handled the entire App Store process alone, including store listings in 5 languages, privacy disclosures, and app review, plus Apple's paid apps agreement, bank account, U.S. W-8BEN tax form, and Taiwan tax questionnaire, and applied for the App Store Small Business Program.
proj.b5: Cost and marketing: Kept costs to the Apple Developer fee by using free tiers for everything else; built a website in 5 languages, planned Threads posts and promotional graphics, and set up tracking links by download source.
proj.a1: A read-it-later app for iPhone and iPad. Share a post or screenshot you want to keep, and AI writes a summary and sorts it; restaurants and places are pinned on a map.
proj.a2: I often saved useful posts and information, then rarely looked at them again. Many similar apps did not support Chinese and lacked features I wanted, such as automatic categorization. After watching an app-building tutorial from the Taiwanese channel Papaya Computer Classroom, I decided to build my own, so that what I saved could be organized more effectively, and to see how far someone with no programming background could go.
proj.a3: Claude Code wrote the code. I came up with the idea, decided which features to build, wrote the development plan and test steps for every feature, checked each one on real devices, and handled the launch, business paperwork, and marketing.
proj.a4: Ask questions about your saved items in plain language (“Ask your notes”); weekly review reminders and a home-screen widget; use your own Google Gemini key or on-device Apple Intelligence; nine theme colors, with the app icon changing to match; import from other apps, and restore deleted items from the trash within 30 days.
proj.a5: Making it stand out among many similar apps. After launch, I planned Threads posts, made promotional graphics, built an official website in five languages, and set up tracking links by download source.
proj.a6: Working with AI comes down to describing what you need precisely. Code is only one part of taking a product from idea to launch; the store listing, privacy, taxes, and marketing were all mine to handle. You only know whether something works once you have tested it yourself, and asking friends and family to try it and listening to their feedback matters too.

res.label: 05 — Research
res.heading: Interviews, experiments & media analysis
res.q.question: The question
res.r1.title: How Digital Technology Shapes Emotional Expression in Chinese Families
res.r1.summary: Semi-structured interviews. I co-designed the interview guide with teammates; interviewed 2 participants, transcribed and coded 2 transcripts, and applied thematic analysis; and wrote the literature review, research aims, methods, results, and limitations sections of the written report.
res.r1.a1: Chinese families often leave love unspoken. Once students leave home for college, do LINE messages and stickers make it easier to say how they feel?
res.r1.a2: Team of 4. We conducted semi-structured in-depth interviews with 8 college students aged 21–23, transcribed the recordings, and analyzed them with thematic analysis.
res.r1.a3: Developed the topic and interview guide with my teammates; interviewed 2 participants and transcribed and coded 2 transcripts; gave the midterm oral presentation. In the written report, I wrote the literature review, research aims, methods, results, and limitations, and formatted the full report.
res.r1.a4: Most families still “do more than they say,” showing care by sending money or asking “what are you up to?” Stickers and text ease the awkwardness of saying thank you or I love you, but text lacks tone, so negative feelings are easily misread, and read receipts add pressure to reply.
res.r1.a5: The topic came from my own experience. My chat with my dad opened almost only when I needed living expenses, and when I wanted to say thanks, I just sent a sticker. The hardest part of interviewing was asking questions without leading the participant.
res.r1.a6: Online counseling has begun to appear in clinical practice, yet people on either side of a screen cannot truly make eye contact. I want to understand how trust is built through digital tools.
res.r2.title: Effects of Vertical vs. Horizontal Stripes on Perceived Body Size
res.r2.summary: Psychology experiment. I co-wrote the research proposal and the informed consent form with my teammates, and proofread the study documents.
res.r2.a1: Horizontal stripes are said to make you look bigger and vertical ones slimmer, yet illusion research finds horizontal stripes look narrower. Does that hold across body types?
res.r2.a2: Team of 5. We built 3D models of women with four different hip sizes, dressed each in vertical and horizontal stripes, showed them in pairs on screen, and asked college students to pick the slimmer-looking one.
res.r2.a3: Co-wrote the experiment proposal, proofread study documents, and prepared the informed consent form.
res.r2.a4: Stripes strongly affected the two slimmer body types but barely changed the two fuller ones; the standard body type actually looked slimmest in vertical stripes, contrary to the illusion theory; male and female participants did not differ significantly.
res.r2.a5: In the consent form, we spelled out anonymous data collection, confidentiality, and the right to withdraw at any time without giving a reason, so participants could take part with peace of mind. When our results did not match the theory, we looked back and found that how the instructions defined “slim” was enough to change the outcome. In a rigorous experiment every word has to be precise, and a small slip can throw off the results. That is what I find hardest about research.
res.r3.title: The Social Construction of Youth Suicide in News Media
res.r3.summary: Individual study. Analyzed how 80 news reports and reader op-eds on youth suicide from three outlets (2019–2021) presented motives and took stances, and proposed recommendations for better reporting.
res.r3.a1: Suicide is the second leading cause of death among 15- to 24-year-olds in Taiwan. How does the news report youth suicide, and how do readers respond?
res.r3.a2: An individual study completed in my first year. I collected 80 news reports and reader op-eds on youth suicide from United Daily News, Liberty Times, and China Times (2019–2021), and categorized them by reported motive and stance.
res.r3.a3: Under my advisor’s guidance, I carried out the data collection, categorization, analysis, and writing, and presented a poster at the 2023 College of Humanities and Social Sciences undergraduate research poster competition, receiving an Honorable Mention.
res.r3.a4: 28% of reports gave no motive at all; the media focused more on what happened than on why. The most common stances were alert and warning, and education and prevention. I also proposed improvements: report more on causes and take more varied stances, since bereaved families may most need concern and compassion.
res.r3.a5: After seeing those statistics in my first year, I wanted to know how the news talked about this. Reading 80 reports made me wonder how a teenager going through a hard time would feel reading them. From choosing a topic and collecting data to presenting, I went through the full research process.
res.r3.a6: This study got me thinking about whether young people’s struggles can be noticed before a crisis happens.

faq.label: 07 — Passenger FAQ
faq.q1: Why did you switch from social work to psychology?
faq.a1: When I took Introduction to Psychology in my first year, I found myself more drawn to psychology and wanting to put empathy to use. Comparing the two, I felt a psychologist's work matched my idea of helping people better, so I transferred to the psychology department. My year in social work got me thinking early about how people interact with social systems, and that interest carried on into the early intervention program I later completed.
faq.q2: Why do you want to become a child clinical psychologist?
faq.a2: While completing the early intervention program, I came to believe in the importance of early identification and early intervention: the sooner someone notices what a child needs, the better their chance to grow up well. Later, at a youth representatives' workshop, I watched young people push past their limits in just a few days, and it made me sure I want to be someone who walks alongside them as they grow.
